title: Trump: 1pm: Pipe bombs, a riot, and the Senate Sergeant at Arms refuses to call the National Guard

description_short: Trump: 1pm: Pipe bombs, a riot, and the Senate Sergeant at Arms refuses to call the National Guard
description_medium: At 1 p.m. on January 6, 2021, Capitol Police Chief Steven Sund asked House Sergeant at Arms Paul Irving to authorize National Guard support, then made the same request to Senate Sergeant at Arms Michael Stenger at 1:05 p.m. The request came as rioters breached the Capitol during Congress’s electoral vote count.
description_long: On January 6, 2021, as rioters attacked the U.S. Capitol and Congress met to count electoral votes, Capitol Police Chief Steven Sund sought National Guard assistance. The New York Times timeline places the request at Sund asked House Sergeant at Arms Paul Irving to declare an emergency and call in the Guard. At 1:05 p.m., he made the same request to Senate Sergeant at Arms Michael Stenger. The timing matters because the request came during a fast-moving breach, when congressional offices and lawmakers were under threat. The episode later became central to investigations of security preparations and the chain of command at the Capitol. The title characterizes Stenger as refusing the request, but the cited timeline establishes when Sund made it without detailing Stenger’s response. The precise decision process and reasons for delay require fuller documentation. The event illustrates how responsibility for emergency assistance was divided among Capitol security officials during the attack.

title: Musk's DOGE Given Access to $6 Trillion Treasury Payment System
description_short: Musk's DOGE Given Access to $6 Trillion Treasury Payment System
description_medium: In early February 2025, Treasury gave a DOGE-affiliated technology executive read-only access to federal payment systems that disburse more than $6 trillion annually. The systems handle payments including Social Security, Medicare, and federal salaries. Treasury said the access was read-only; critics raised privacy and security concerns, and career official David Lebryk resigned.
description_long: In early February 2025, Treasury granted a DOGE-affiliated technology executive read-only access to federal payment systems. Those systems process more than $6 trillion in annual disbursements, including Social Security, Medicare, and federal payroll. Treasury told lawmakers the access was read-only. The decision prompted concern because the systems contain sensitive financial and personal information and are essential to routine government payments. The access dispute also coincided with the resignation of David Lebryk, a senior career Treasury official. Democrats and security experts warned that access to sensitive system data could create privacy and cybersecurity risks, while the administration described the access as limited. Read-only access does not itself authorize changing or stopping payments; the concerns centered on the scope of information available and the safeguards around it. The episode became part of wider legal and congressional scrutiny of DOGE’s access to government data. The $6 trillion figure refers to annual payment throughput, not an account balance or new spending authority. Treasury’s “read-only” characterization was disputed by critics concerned about the scope of access and safeguards.

title: Trump Guts CDC, Fires Dozens of Public Health Officials
description_short: Trump Guts CDC, Fires Dozens of Public Health Officials
description_medium: In late February 2025, the Trump administration fired or placed on administrative leave dozens of senior CDC officials, including leaders of its infectious disease and emergency response divisions. Entire research programs were defunded. The pandemic preparedness infrastructure rebuilt after COVID-19 was systematically dismantled. Public health officials warned the US was left significantly less prepared for emerging infectious disease threats. The gutting of CDC came alongside cuts to NIH research funding and elimination of the White House pandemic preparedness office established under Biden.
description_long: It also describes research-program defunding and changes to pandemic-preparedness infrastructure rebuilt after COVID-19. Public-health officials warned that the losses left the country less prepared for new infectious threats. The event concerns reductions in government capacity and the warnings they generated, rather than a measured outbreak outcome attributed to those reductions. Staffing changes, program funding and the ability to organize a response are related but distinct parts of preparedness. That wider context helps explain why the warnings extended beyond one agency. The record does not quantify a precise change in national readiness or establish that a particular later epidemic resulted from the personnel decisions.

title: Chris Wright Energy Secretary Accelerates Fossil Fuels and Kills Clean Energy Programs

description_short: Chris Wright Energy Secretary Accelerates Fossil Fuels and Kills Clean Energy Programs
description_medium: Energy Secretary Chris Wright — a former fracking company CEO who had publicly denied climate change — aggressively accelerated fossil fuel production permits and approvals while terminating, reversing, or defunding clean energy programs funded by the Inflation Reduction Act. Wright used the Department of Energy to serve the interests of the oil and gas industry he had led, implementing policies that industry lobbyists had written. Climate scientists warned the energy policy reversal locked in catastrophic warming scenarios that would be impossible to reverse.
description_long: On February 5, 2025, Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed an order directing the Department of Energy to implement Trump’s energy agenda. The department’s announcement emphasized expanding energy production, reducing regulatory barriers, and shifting away from policies aimed at net-zero emissions. The order framed energy abundance as a goal for the department. The order states the department’s priorities but does not identify specific clean-energy program cancellations, show that industry lobbyists wrote its policies, or establish climate effects. Those broader claims require evidence about particular program decisions and their consequences. The order alone documents a policy direction favoring increased energy production; the effects on individual clean-energy initiatives remain unclear.

title: Six National Monuments Targeted for Mining and Drilling
description_short: Six National Monuments Targeted for Mining and Drilling
description_medium: In February 2025, Interior Secretary Burgum ordered a review of all national monuments for potential boundary reductions to enable energy and mining development. By April 2025, Interior aides were actively analyzing geological maps to assess six monuments for shrinkage: Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante in Utah, Baaj Nwaavjo I'tah Kukveni-Ancestral Footprints of the Grand Canyon and Ironwood Forest in Arizona, Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks in New Mexico, and Chuckwalla in California. Grand Staircase-Escalante holds large coal reserves; Bears Ears contains uranium deposits.
description_long: In February 2025, Interior Secretary Burgum ordered a review of all national monuments for potential boundary reductions to enable energy and mining development. Grand Staircase-Escalante holds large coal reserves; Bears Ears contains uranium deposits. The monuments collectively protect millions of acres of Indigenous sacred land and unique ecosystems. title: Trump Endorses Election Deniers in 12+ States — Many Lose General Elections
description_short: Trump Endorses Election Deniers in 12+ States — Many Lose General Elections
description_medium: Following the 2020 election, Trump systematically endorsed candidates who refused to accept Biden's 2020 victory as a condition of political support, effectively making election denial a litmus test for Republican candidates across the country. In the 2022 elections, Trump-endorsed election deniers ran for secretary of state and governor positions in key battleground states including Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Nevada, and Georgia. The majority of these candidates lost in general elections, costing Republicans winnable races and contributing to the underperformance of the 2022 Republican ticket.
description_long: Following the 2020 election, Trump systematically endorsed candidates who refused to accept Biden's 2020 victory as a condition of political support, effectively making election denial a litmus test for Republican candidates across the country. In the 2022 elections, Trump-endorsed election deniers ran for secretary of state and governor positions in key battleground states including Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Nevada, and Georgia. The majority of these candidates lost in general elections, costing Republicans winnable races and contributing to the underperformance of the 2022 Republican ticket. Political analysts attributed the losses in part to voters rejecting extreme positions on election integrity. The offices at issue matter because governors and secretaries of state can have responsibilities affecting election administration. The cited losses concern particular races, rather than proof that every candidate endorsed by Trump lost or that every voter rejected him for the same reason. Analysts' explanations of the result should remain interpretations.

title: Trump Secretly Funds Anti-Casino Ads to Block Mohawk Competition
description_short: Trump Secretly Funds Anti-Casino Ads to Block Mohawk Competition
description_medium: In 2000, a lobbying group called the 'Institute for Law and Safety' ran inflammatory newspaper ads in upstate New York opposing a proposed Mohawk Nation casino, featuring images of needles and cocaine. The ads were secretly funded by Donald Trump, who stood to lose business at his Atlantic City casinos if the Mohawk casino opened. The New York State Lobbying Commission investigated and fined Trump $250,000 — at the time the largest fine in the commission's history — for failing to register as a lobbyist and for the deceptive funding.
description_long: In 2000, a lobbying group called the 'Institute for Law and Safety' ran inflammatory newspaper ads in upstate New York opposing a proposed Mohawk Nation casino, featuring images of needles and cocaine. The ads were secretly funded by Donald Trump, who stood to lose business at his Atlantic City casinos if the Mohawk casino opened. The New York State Lobbying Commission investigated and fined Trump $250,000 — at the time the largest fine in the commission's history — for failing to register as a lobbyist and for the deceptive funding. Trump had hired political operative Roger Stone to manage the campaign. The financial interest behind the advertisements is part of the episode's significance: a casino competitor funded advocacy presented under another organization's name. The lobbying commission's fine was an identifiable regulatory response to disclosure and registration failures. The inflammatory imagery and the business competition are distinct from a finding about the Mohawk Nation itself.

title: Trump Pardons Corrupt GOP Congressmen Collins and Hunter
description_short: Trump Pardons Corrupt GOP Congressmen Collins and Hunter
description_medium: In December 2020, Trump pardoned former Representative Chris Collins, who had pleaded guilty to insider trading charges for leaking confidential drug trial information to his son, and former Representative Duncan Hunter, who had pleaded guilty to misappropriating more than $250,000 in campaign funds for personal expenses including family vacations, a flight for his pet rabbit, and extramarital affairs. Both had been early congressional supporters of Trump's 2016 campaign, and both had already resigned from Congress in disgrace.

Both had been early congressional supporters of Trump's 2016 campaign, and both had already resigned from Congress in disgrace. title: Trump's Years-Long Campaign of Misogynist Attacks on Rosie O'Donnell
description_short: Trump's Years-Long Campaign of Misogynist Attacks on Rosie O'Donnell
description_medium: Beginning in December 2006 when O'Donnell criticized him on The View, Trump launched a sustained multi-year campaign of sexist and body-shaming attacks against her, calling her a 'fat pig,' 'disgusting,' 'a loser,' and 'a slob' in television interviews, press statements, and eventually on Twitter. Trump declared she had 'a fat, ugly face' and claimed she was 'a degenerate.' The attacks spanned from 2006 through the 2016 presidential campaign, where Trump invoked O'Donnell at the first Republican debate. Mental health advocates noted the relentless targeting was a form of public bullying.

title: Trump Calls Kamala Harris a 'Monster' and 'Communist'
description_short: Trump Calls Kamala Harris a 'Monster' and 'Communist'
description_medium: In October 2020, during the final weeks of the presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly called then-Senator and Democratic vice-presidential candidate Kamala Harris a 'monster,' a 'communist,' and a 'madwoman' in rally speeches and interviews. Trump described Harris as 'not a competent person' and used the word 'monster' unprompted in an October 9, 2020 Oval Office interview. The attacks intensified as the 2024 campaign against Harris's own presidential run approached, with Trump and allies deploying a cascade of dehumanizing descriptors.
description_long: In October 2020, during the final weeks of the presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly called then-Senator and Democratic vice-presidential candidate Kamala Harris a 'monster,' a 'communist,' and a 'madwoman' in rally speeches and interviews. The attacks intensified as the 2024 campaign against Harris's own presidential run approached, with Trump and allies deploying a cascade of dehumanizing descriptors. title: Trump White House stops releasing visitor logs, permanently
description_short: Trump White House stops releasing visitor logs, permanently
description_medium: On April 14, 2017, the Trump White House ended the Obama-era practice of voluntarily publishing visitor logs. Officials cited national security and policy-development concerns, while watchdog groups said secrecy would make it harder to track attempts to influence the administration. The change concerned public access to visitor records; the linked timeline notes that Biden later reversed the practice in 2021.
description_long: The Trump White House announced on April 14, 2017 that it would stop voluntarily releasing visitor logs, ending a transparency practice used during Barack Obama’s administration. Officials cited national security concerns and argued that publication could interfere with policy development. They also pointed to the practices of administrations preceding Obama. Watchdog groups criticized the decision because visitor records could help identify people and organizations seeking to influence White House decisions. Their criticism was about public accountability, rather than proof that every meeting concealed improper conduct. The administration defended its broader approach to openness partly by citing expanded access to the press briefing room, although briefing access and disclosure of private visitors serve different purposes. The linked timeline says the logs remained confidential during Trump’s tenure and that the Biden administration reversed the approach in 2021. That later change limits the preserved title’s claim of permanence.
